title: Evals: golden datasets, CI gates and LLM-as-judge
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Golden datasets, regression suites with pytest, CI thresholds, LLM-as-judge rubrics and biases, calibration against human labels, and the Ragas, DeepEval and Langfuse tooling.
source: Zheng et al. MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (NeurIPS 2023); Ragas, DeepEval and Langfuse docs; tau-bench (Yao et al.); Codex paper (Chen et al.) for pass@k; pytest docs

questions.prompt: Your golden suite has 200 cases and the CI gate requires a pass rate of at least 92%. What is the maximum number of failing cases that still lets the build pass?
questions.explanation: 92% of 200 is 184 passes, so at most 200 - 184 = 16 failures are tolerated. Many teams also gate on per-category minimums so a critical category cannot hide inside the average.

questions.prompt: Write a pytest test named test_golden_pass_rate that calls run_eval() (it returns a list of dicts, each with a boolean key "passed") and fails the build if the pass rate is below 0.9.

checks.label: divides by the number of results

questions.model:
def test_golden_pass_rate():
    results = run_eval()
    rate = sum(r["passed"] for r in results) / len(results)
    assert rate >= 0.9, f"pass rate {rate:.0%}"
questions.explanation: Other forms pass (statistics.mean, numpy, asserting on a precomputed number of failures). Put a message in the assert so the CI log says what failed.

questions.prompt: Write a parametrized pytest that loads a list of cases from golden.json (each has "id", "question" and "expected_contains") and, for each, asserts that answer(question) contains expected_contains ignoring case. Use the case id as the test id.
questions.explanation: Each case becomes its own test, so the CI report names the exact failing case. Other correct forms (re.search with IGNORECASE) pass.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: For regression runs you should pin the model snapshot and use temperature 0.
questions.reason: Provider aliases can point at newer model versions over time, and sampling adds run-to-run variation.

whys.a: Correct: both effects make results flaky or drift silently, so pinning removes them (temperature 0 reduces but may not fully eliminate non-determinism).
whys.b: R is not a side fact; it is the reason pinning is advised.
whys.c: R is true: floating aliases do move.
whys.d: A is true; pinning is standard practice.

questions.explanation: Also record prompt version, retrieval index version and dataset version with each run so results are comparable.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: LLM judges tend to prefer longer answers, which is called verbosity bias.
questions.reason: Verbosity bias disappears once the judge prompt says to be objective and fair.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation.
whys.b: R is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (documented in the MT-Bench work), but a polite instruction alone does not remove it; use rubrics, length controls and human calibration.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Mitigations: criteria-based rubrics, penalise padding explicitly, compare against reference answers, and check score vs length correlation.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In pairwise judging, running each comparison in both orders (A,B then B,A) reduces position bias.
questions.reason: A judge can be calibrated against human labels by measuring agreement with Cohen's kappa.

whys.a: R is true but it concerns calibration, not order effects, so it does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: swapping removes first-position preference (A true), and kappa-based calibration (R true) is a separate technique.
whys.c: R is true: kappa corrects raw agreement for chance.
whys.d: A is true; inconsistent verdicts across orders are usually treated as ties.

questions.explanation: If the verdict flips when the order flips, treat it as a tie or as low-confidence.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A model is an unbiased judge of its own outputs.
questions.reason: Judges often score text that resembles their own style or wording more favourably (self-preference bias).

whys.a: A is false, so no reason can make this pair correct.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because of self-preference bias, and R is true. Prefer a different or stronger judge model family and verify with humans.

questions.explanation: Zheng et al. (MT-Bench) call this self-enhancement bias; later work calls it self-preference. Use a judge from a different family than the generator where possible, and spot-check with human labels.

questions.prompt: A judge and a human agree on 90% of 100 labelled answers. By chance alone the expected agreement is 50%. Compute Cohen's kappa = (observed - expected) / (1 - expected), multiplied by 100.
questions.explanation: (0.90 - 0.50) / (1 - 0.50) = 0.80. Kappa discounts agreement that would happen by luck, which matters when one label dominates.

questions.prompt: Which judge prompt design gives the most reliable and debuggable scores for a support-bot answer?

options.text: Separate criteria with anchored definitions per score level, reasoning first, then a score.
options.why: Right: anchored rubrics and short rationale reduce noise and make failures inspectable.

options.text: "Rate the answer from 1 to 10 for overall quality." with no further instruction at all given to the judge model.
options.why: Vague scales produce noisy, clustered scores that drift between runs.

options.text: Ask the judge to reply with only the number, hiding its reasoning, so that scores are cheaper to generate for every case.
options.why: Hiding the rationale saves little and makes the verdicts impossible to audit.

options.text: Show the judge the candidate model name so it can account for what that model usually does well or badly.
options.why: Revealing identity adds bias; judges should be blind to the source.

questions.explanation: Keep scales small (pass/fail or 1-5 with anchors), judge one criterion per call where possible, and version the rubric like code.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong in calibrating an LLM judge before you trust it in CI? Select all that apply.

options.text: Have humans label a stratified sample of real outputs.
options.why: Right: you need ground truth to measure against.

options.text: Measure agreement (kappa or per-class precision/recall) and iterate on the rubric.
options.why: Right: tune the prompt and examples until agreement is acceptable.

options.text: Skip human labels if the judge model is the largest available.
options.why: Size does not prove it matches your quality bar.

options.text: Accept the judge after it looks sensible on three examples.

questions.explanation: Re-check calibration when the judge model, rubric or traffic mix changes.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or technique to its role.

right.text: RAG metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevancy and context precision/recall
Unit-test-style LLM metrics (for example G-Eval) that run under pytest
Tracing plus datasets, scores and LLM-as-judge evaluators in a UI
Test runner whose exit code gates the CI pipeline

questions.explanation: Tools overlap, so describe the role you need (metrics, test harness, observability) and pick accordingly.

questions.text: A golden set should include {1} questions, edge cases and past {2}; run a small subset on every pull request and the full suite {3}.
questions.explanation: Add each real incident as a new case with the expected behaviour so it can never regress silently. Version the dataset.

questions.prompt: True or false: with temperature 0 an LLM judge is guaranteed to return the same score every run.

options.why: Even at temperature 0, batching and hardware effects can change outputs.
Correct: determinism is not guaranteed, and a provider model update can change scores, so repeat borderline cases and pin versions.

questions.explanation: Estimate judge noise by re-scoring a sample several times.

questions.prompt: True or false: a RAG faithfulness metric (does the answer follow from the retrieved context) can be computed without a ground-truth answer.

options.why: Correct: it compares the answer against the retrieved context, so no reference answer is required.
It needs context and answer, not a gold answer.

questions.explanation: Reference-free metrics are useful for online monitoring on unlabeled traffic, but still need calibration.

questions.prompt: A code agent is sampled n = 10 times on a task and c = 3 samples pass. Using the unbiased pass@k estimator 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k) from the Codex paper, compute pass@2 multiplied by 100, rounded to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: C(7,2) = 21 and C(10,2) = 45, so pass@2 = 1 - 21/45 = 0.533, i.e. 53. pass@k asks whether at least one of k tries succeeds, whereas pass^k (tau-bench) asks whether all k succeed.

questions.prompt: Match each LLM-as-judge weakness reported by Zheng et al. to a standard mitigation.

left.text: Weak grading of maths and reasoning answers

right.text: Judge both orders and treat a flip as a tie
Rubric that penalises padding, and check score against length
Use a judge from a different model family than the generator
Give the judge a reference answer or ask it to solve the task first

questions.explanation: The MT-Bench paper proposes swapping positions, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought and reference-guided judging; the rest are practitioner extensions.
